summary:
Mari El is a republic of the Russian Federation and stands under Russia's national framework, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Russia banned legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The UK government country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the framework under which Mari El operates: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the "gay propaganda" law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Under that note, LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, the standard applied to UK asylum claims.

Federal "extremism" enforcement documented by Human Rights Watch on 30 June 2025 applies nationwide, Mari El included. Russian courts have issued 101 "extremism"-related convictions for participating in the "international LGBT movement" or displaying its alleged symbols, and 81 people across 98 court cases since January 2024 have been convicted of administrative offences for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. The 2023 Supreme Court designation enabled criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison, building on the 2013 "gay propaganda" law.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and "extremism" prosecutions. Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented: BBC Russian (27 July 2024) reported on "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

Mari El is one republic within a nationwide pattern, and no republic-level enforcement record for Mari El appears in the source inventory. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mari El live under the same federal statutes as the rest of Russia: legal gender recognition is unavailable, gender-affirming care is prohibited, and displaying symbols of the designated "international LGBT movement", largely on social media, draws administrative charges that have produced 81 convictions across 98 court cases since January 2024.

Repeat propaganda offences can escalate to criminal prosecution carrying up to four years' imprisonment, while extremism-related provisions permit sentences of up to 12 years. The UK country policy note recognises LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as a particular social group under the refugee convention, which governs UK asylum determinations.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Mari El-specific enforcement figures, court records, or republic-level decrees on gender identity appear in the source inventory; the counts cited here are national Russian totals and are not broken down by subject of the federation.

The inventory does not resolve whether Mari El maintains its own regional "propaganda" rules or hate-crime provisions beyond the federal statutes, and no reporting on violence against transgender people located in Mari El itself was available for this pass.

Access to documentation, police conduct toward transgender detainees, and the availability of legal or medical assistance in Mari El are not sourced and remain unresolved.
